title: PostgreSQL 17 Documentation, 28.1. Reliability
why: Authoritative account of why a partially written page can be repaired from full page images recorded in the WAL and of the CRC-32C protection on every WAL record.

title: ARIES: A Transaction Recovery Method Supporting Fine-Granularity Locking and Partial Rollbacks Using Write-Ahead Logging
version: ACM Transactions on Database Systems 17(1):94-162, March 1992 (PDF read via people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~brewer/cs262/Aries.pdf)
why: The canonical write-ahead-logging recovery algorithm; best for why redo during replay must be idempotent and how the per-page LSN enforces it.

claim: WAL's defining rule is that changes to the data files must be written only after the changes have been logged and the log records flushed to permanent storage.
quote: Briefly, WAL's central concept is that changes to data files (where tables and indexes reside) must be written only after those changes have been logged, that is, after WAL records describing the changes have been flushed to permanent storage.

locator: section 28.1 Reliability, paragraph on partial disk-platter writes
claim: Because PostgreSQL writes a full image of a page into the WAL before modifying that page on disk, crash recovery can rebuild a page whose disk write was only partially completed.
quote: To guard against such failures, PostgreSQL periodically writes full page images to permanent WAL storage *before* modifying the actual page on disk. By doing this, during crash recovery PostgreSQL can restore partially-written pages from WAL.

locator: section 28.1 Reliability, bulleted list of storage protections, first bullet
claim: Every WAL record carries a CRC-32C checksum that is checked during crash recovery, so an incompletely or incorrectly written record can be detected instead of being replayed as if it were complete.
quote: Each individual record in a WAL file is protected by a CRC-32C (32-bit) check that allows us to tell if record contents are correct. The CRC value is set when we write each WAL record and checked during crash recovery, archive recovery and replication.

locator: section 3.8 Persisted state and server restarts
claim: After a restart a persistent Raft state machine has already applied most log entries, so the last applied index must be persisted to avoid applying those entries a second time.
quote: A persistent state machine, however, has already applied most entries after a restart; to avoid reapplying them, its last applied index must also be persistent.

claim: ARIES makes redo idempotent by consulting the LSN stored on each page to decide whether a logged operation still needs to be redone.
quote: Idempotence of operations is ensured since the LSN on each page is used to determine whether an operation should be redone or not.

claim: Only the WAL file must be flushed to disk to make a transaction durable, rather than every data file the transaction changed, which is why commit can sync the WAL alone.
quote: Using WAL results in a significantly reduced number of disk writes, because only the WAL file needs to be flushed to disk to guarantee that a transaction is committed, rather than every data file changed by the transaction.

claim: SQLite's atomic-commit procedure assumes a sector write may be interrupted part-way so that only a portion of the sector is changed, though the write is assumed to run linearly from one end of the sector.
quote: SQLite has traditionally assumed that a sector write is not atomic. However, SQLite does always assume that a sector write is linear.

locator: section 2 Hardware Assumptions, paragraph on the VFS xDeviceCharacteristics method
claim: A VFS may declare that sector writes are atomic, in which case SQLite exploits it, but the default Unix and Windows VFSes do not, so SQLite normally assumes non-atomic sector writes.
quote: The xDeviceCharacteristics method might indicate that sector writes are atomic, and if it does so indicate, SQLite will try to take advantage of that fact. But the default xDeviceCharacteristics method for both Unix and Windows does not indicate atomic sector writes and so these optimizations are normally omitted.
